# Angular Momentum

We will review the theory of angular momentum in quantum mechanics, largely
following the treatment in @sakurai1986modern.

## Rotation in classical mechanics
It is well-known that a body initially at a point $\bv{r}$ when first
translated by $\bv{x}_1$ and then by $\bv{x}_2$ reaches the same position if
we had first translated it by $\bv{x}_2$ and then by $\bv{x}_1$. This is
because the result of two translation is an addition of vectors, a commutative
operation.

Rotations cannot be described by vectors. If a vector $\bv{x} =
[x_1, x_2, x_3]^T$ is rotated then its components after rotation $[x_1^\op,
x_2^\op, x_3^\op]^T$ are related to its original components by
$$
\begin{bmatrix}x_1^\op \\ x_2^\op \\ x_3^\op\end{bmatrix} =
R\begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-am1}
If $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the matrices representing two rotations and if they
happen one after the other then their combined effect is represented by either
$R_2R_1$ or $R_1R_2$. Unlike addition of vectors, the multiplication of
matrices is \emph{not} commutative.

We shall follow the convention of interpreting a rotation as the act of moving
a vector keeping the coordinate systems untouched. With this convention, a
rotation of a vector by and angle $\phi$ about the three axes is represented
by
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
R_x(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\
0 & \sin\phi & \cos\phi
\end{bmatrix}  \\
R_y(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}\cos\phi & 0 & \sin\phi \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
-\sin\phi & 0 & \cos\phi
\end{bmatrix}  \\
R_z(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}\cos\phi & -\sin\phi & 0 \\
\sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix} 
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-am2}
Note that the negative sign of $\sin\phi$ appears in the "$y$ row" for $R_x$,
"$z$ row" for $R_y$ and "$x$ row" for $R_z$.

If $\phi$ is infinitesimally small then we can write the above equations as
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
R_x(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 - \phi^2/2 & -\phi \\
0 & \phi & 1 - \phi^2/2
\end{bmatrix}  \\
R_y(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}1 - \phi^2/2 & 0 & \phi \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
-\phi & 0 & 1 - \phi^2/2
\end{bmatrix}  \\
R_z(\phi) &=& \begin{bmatrix}1 - \phi^2/2 & -\phi & 0 \\
\phi & 1 - \phi^2/2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix} 
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-am3}
so that
$$
R_xR_y - R_yR_x = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -\phi^2 & 0 \\
\phi^2 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = R_z(\phi^2) - I,
$$ {#eq-am4}
where we ignored terms of $O(\phi^3)$ and above. In fact, if we ignore terms
of $O(\phi^2)$ and above then
$$
R_xR_y - R_yR_x = 0 \text{ up to } O(\phi).
$$ {#eq-am5}
Thus, even if finite rotations do not commute, infinitesimal ones do. Can we
express infinitesimal rotations as vectors?

## Infinitesimal rotations as vectors
We notice that the matrix $R_z(\phi^2)$ is anti-symmetric. We will now argue
that every infinitisemal rotation is represented by an anti-symmetric matrix.
If $R$ is one such then we can write its effect on a vector $\bv{x}$ as
$$
\bv{x}^\prime = (1 + R)\bv{x}.
$$ {#eq-am6}
It is clear that, up to first order, the inverse of the transformation $1 + R$
is $1 - R$. We also know that rotation matrices are always orthogonal, that is
their transpose is their inverse. Therefore, for infinitesimal rotations, we
have \cite{wolfram1}
$$
(1 + R)^T = (1 - R) \Rightarrow R^T = -R,
$$ {#eq-am7}
that is, $R$ is anti-symmetric. An anti-symmetric matrix has only three
independent entries and is therefore isomorphic to a vector. One can represent
a general infinitesimal rotation as
$$
R = \begin{bmatrix}0 & d\Omega_3 & -d\Omega_2 \\
-d\Omega_3 & 0 & d\Omega_1 \\
d\Omega_2 & -d\Omega_1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-am8}
so that
$$
\begin{bmatrix}x_1^\prime \\ x_2^\prime \\ x_3^\prime \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}0 & d\Omega_3 & -d\Omega_2 \\
-d\Omega_3 & 0 & d\Omega_1 \\
d\Omega_2 & -d\Omega_1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}
x_2d\Omega_3 - x_3d\Omega_2 \\
x_3d\Omega_1 - x_1d\Omega_3 \\
x_2d\Omega_2 - x_2d\Omega_1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-am9}
We can write this equation succintly as
$$
x_i^\prime = \epsilon_{ijk}x_jd\Omega_k
$$ {#eq-am10}
which allows us to consider $[d\Omega_1, d\Omega_2, d\Omega_3]^T$ as a vector.
We can write equation @eq-am10 as
$$
\bv{x}^\prime = \bv{x} \times d\bv{\Omega}.
$$ {#eq-am11}

## Rotation in quantum mechanics
We know from classical mechanics that the momentum is a generator of 
infinitesimal translations, the hamiltonian is a generator of infinitesimal
time evolution and the angular momentum is a generator of infinitesimal 
rotation. Furthermore, the products of momentum and translation, energy and
time interval and angular momentum and angular displacement all have the 
dimension of action. Therefore, an operator representing an infinitesimal change
can be written as 
$$
U_\epsilon = 1 - iG\epsilon
$$ {#eq-am12}
where $G$ is an operator of such dimensions that $G\epsilon$ is dimensionless.
In the case of infinitesimal translation $\delta x$ along the $x$ axis, we have
$$
U_{\delta x} = 1 - i\frac{p_x}{\hbar}\delta x
$$ {#eq-am13}
while in the case of a time evolution by $\delta t$, we have
$$
U_{\delta t} = 1 - i\frac{H}{\hbar}\delta t.
$$ {#eq-am14}
Carrying this analogy, we write the operator for an infinitesimal rotation
about the $k$ axis as 
$$
U_{\delta\phi} = 1 - i\frac{J_k}{\hbar}\delta\phi,
$$ {#eq-am15}
where $J_k$ is the angular momentum operator. In general, for a rotation about
a unit vector $\un$ by an angle $\delta\phi$, we can write
$$
D(\hat{\bv{n}}, \delta\phi) = 1 - i\frac{\bv{J}\cdot\un}{\hbar}\delta\phi.
$$ {#eq-am16}
A finite rotation by angle $\phi$ can be considered to be made up of $n$
infinitesimal rotations in steps of $\phi/n$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Thus,
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
D(\un,\phi) &=& 
\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\prod D\left(\un, \frac{\phi}{n}\right) \\
 &=&
\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(1 - i\frac{\bv{J}\cdot\un}{\hbar}\frac{\phi}
{n}\right)^n \\
 &=& \exp\left(-i\frac{\bv{J}\cdot\un}{\hbar}\phi\right).
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am17}
Using @eq-am16, we have
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
D(\bv{e}_x,\delta\phi) &=& 1 - i\frac{J_x}{\hbar}\delta\phi \\
D(\bv{e}_y,\delta\phi) &=& 1 - i\frac{J_y}{\hbar}\delta\phi \\ 
D(\bv{e}_z,\delta\phi^2) &=& 1 - i\frac{J_z}{\hbar}\delta\phi^2 
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am18}
so that
$$
D(\bv{e}_x,\delta\phi)D(\bv{e}_y,\delta\phi) - 
D(\bv{e}_y,\delta\phi)D(\bv{e}_x,\delta\phi) = 
1 - \frac{J_xJ_y - J_yJ_x}{\hbar^2}\delta\phi^2 + O(\delta\phi^4)
$$ {#eq-am19}
Using equation @eq-am4 as an analogy, we can propose that the operators 
representing rotations should obey a similar equation. That is, 
$$
D(\bv{e}_x,\delta\phi)D(\bv{e}_y,\delta\phi) - 
D(\bv{e}_y,\delta\phi)D(\bv{e}_x,\delta\phi) = 
D(\bv{e}_z,\delta\phi^2) - 1 
$$
Using equations @eq-am18 and @eq-am19 we get
$$
1-i\frac{[J_x, J_y]}{\hbar^2}\delta\phi^2 =1 - i\frac{J_z}{\hbar}\delta\phi^2,
$$
that is,
$$
[J_x, J_y] = i\hbar J_z.
$$ {#eq-am20}
Similarly, we can also conclude 
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
[J_y, J_z] &=& i\hbar J_x \\
[J_z, J_x] &=& i\hbar J_y
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am21}
Equations @eq-am20 and @eq-am21 are the familiar commutation relations between
the components of angular momentum. They are derived solely from the observation
that angular momentum is the generator of infinitesimal rotations and the 
matrices which rotate vectors by infinitesimal degrees follow relations similar
to @eq-am4. In particular, we did not use the classical relation $\bv{L} = 
\bv{x} \times \bv{p}$ to derive the operator for angular momentum and the latter
to infer the commutation relations. As a result, equations @eq-am20 and @eq-am21
are valid even in situations where the angular momentum has no classical 
analogue, that is, the spin.

## An overview of spin-$1/2$ systems
Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck explained the Zeeman splitting by proposing that 
electrons have an intrinsic magnentic moment. This idea also explained the 
results of the Stern and Gerlach experiment. Magnetic moments are related to
current loops in classical physics and charges moving in loops possess angular
momentum. Thus, an intrinsic magnetic moment is associated with an intrinsic
angular momentum, which was given the name "spin". Experiments also indicated
that for an electron, there are only two possible values of the spin along a
fixed direction.

The two spin states $\ket{u}$ and $\ket{d}$ are defined in such a way that
$$
S_z\ket{u} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\ket{u},\;S_z\ket{d} = -\frac{\hbar}{2}\ket{d}
$$ {#eq-am22}
where $S_z$ is the $z$-component of the spin angular momentum $\bv{S}$. In the
basis $\{\ket{u}, \ket{d}\}$, the three spin operators are defined as
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
S_x &=& = \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u}\bra{d} + \ket{d}\bra{u}) \\
S_y &=& = -i\frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u}\bra{d} - \ket{d}\bra{u}) \\
S_z &=& = \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u}\bra{u} - \ket{d}\bra{d}) 
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am23}
From these equations, one can readily confirm that
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
S_z\ket{u} &=& \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u}\braket{u|u} - \ket{d}\braket{d|u}) \\
 &=& \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u} \cdot 1 - \ket{d} \cdot 0) \\
 &=& \frac{\hbar}{2}\ket{u}
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am24}
and
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
S_z\ket{d} &=& \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u}\braket{u|d} - \ket{d}\braket{d|d}) \\
 &=& \frac{\hbar}{2}(\ket{u} \cdot 0 - \ket{d} \cdot 1) \\
 &=& -\frac{\hbar}{2}\ket{d}
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-am25}

### Effect of rotation on spin - I

Now assume that a spin-$1/2$ system is in an arbitrary state $\ket{i}$ and is
rotated about the $z$-axis by and angle $\phi$. Let $\ket{f}=D_z(\phi)\ket{i}$.
We want to compute $\langle S_x \rangle$ in the initial state $\ket{i}$ and the
final state $\ket{f}$.
Now,
$$
\braket{S_x}_f = \bra{f}S_x\ket{f} = \bra{i}D_z^\dagger S_x D_z\ket{i}.
$$ {#eq-am26}
Using @eq-am17 and @eq-am23,
$$
D_z^\dagger S_x D_z=\exp\left(\frac{iS_z\phi}{\hbar}\right)\frac{\hbar}{2}
(\ket{u} \bra{d} + \ket{d}\bra{u}) 
\exp\left(\frac{-iS_z\phi}{\hbar}\right)
$$ {#eq-am27}
As
$$
\exp\left(\frac{iS_z\phi}{\hbar}\right) = 
\sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{(iS_z\phi)^n}{\hbar^n},
$$
using @eq-am24, we get
$$
\exp\left(\frac{iS_z\phi}{\hbar}\right)\ket{u} =
\sum_{n \ge 0}\frac{i^n\phi^n}{2^n}\ket{u} = e^{i\phi/2}\ket{u}
$$ {#eq-am28}
and using @eq-am25, we get
$$
\exp\left(\frac{iS_z\phi}{\hbar}\right)\ket{d} =
\sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{(-i)^n\phi^n}{2^n}\ket{d} = e^{-i\phi/2}\ket{d}
$$ {#eq-am29}
Using equations @eq-am28 and @eq-am29 and their respective adjoints in equation
@eq-am27, we get
$$
D_z^\dagger S_x D_z = \frac{\hbar}{2}\left((\ket{u}\bra{d} + \ket{d}\bra{u})
\cos\phi + i(\ket{u}\bra{d} - \ket{d}\bra{u})\sin\phi\right)
$$ {#eq-am30}
Using equations @eq-am23, 
$$
D_z^\dagger S_x D_z = S_x\cos\phi - S_y\sin\phi.
$$ {#eq-am31}
and therefore, from @eq-am26,
$$
\bra{f}S_x\ket{f} = \bra{i}S_x\ket{i}\cos\phi - \bra{i}S_y\ket{i}\sin\phi.
$$
that is
$$
\braket{S_x}_f = \braket{S_x}_i\cos\phi - \braket{S_y}_i\sin\phi.
$$ {#eq-am32}
We can similarly show that
$$
\braket{S_y}_f = \braket{S_x}_i\cos\phi + \braket{S_y}_i\sin\phi.
$$ {#eq-am33}
and
$$
\braket{S_z}_f = \braket{S_z}_i.
$$ {#eq-am34}
We can combine equations @eq-am32, @eq-am33 and @eq-am34 as
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 
\braket{S_x}_f \\ \braket{S_y}_f \\ \braket{S_z}_f
\end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\phi & -\sin\phi & 0 \\ \sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 
\braket{S_x}_i \\ \braket{S_y}_i \\ \braket{S_z}_i
\end{bmatrix} = R_z(\phi)
\begin{bmatrix} 
\braket{S_x}_i \\ \braket{S_y}_i \\ \braket{S_z}_i
\end{bmatrix}. 
$$ {#eq-am35}
Recall that $\ket{f} = D_z(\phi)\ket{i}$. If we interpret the column vectors
as $\bra{i}\bv{S}\ket{i}$ and $\bra{f}\bv{S}\ket{f}$ then equation @eq-am35
suggests that expectation of value of $\bv{S}$ behaves like a classical vector.
The way a classical vector is transformed by $R_z(\phi)$, so is the expectation
of $\bv{S}$ as the rotation operator $D_z(\phi)$ transforms $\ket{i}$ to 
$\ket{f}$. The rotation operator $D_z(\phi)$ when applied to a spin state 
$\ket{i}$ rotates the expectation value of $\bv{S}$ around the $z$-axis.

### Effect of rotation on spin - II
In the previous section we used the form of $S_x$ operator given by @eq-am23.
We will now show that it is possible to derive an analogue of @eq-am35 using 
the commutation relations @eq-am20 and @eq-am21. That is, we will show that
$$
\braket{\bv{J}}_f = R_z(\phi)\braket{\bv{J}}_i.
$$ {#eq-am36}
We will use the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula
$$
e^{-iG\lambda}Ae^{iG\lambda}=\sum_{k \ge 0}\left(\frac{ik}{\lambda}\right)^k
[G,A]_k,
$$ {#eq-am37}
where
$$
[G, A]_k = \begin{cases} A & \text{ if } k = 0 \\ [G, [G, A]_{k-1}] &  
\text{ if } k > 0.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-am38}

If $G = J_z$ and $A = J_x$ then
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
[J_z, J_x]_0 &=& J_x \\
[J_z, J_x]_1 &=& i\hbar J_y \\
[J_z, J_x]_2 &=& (i\hbar)^2 J_x = -\hbar^2 J_x \\
[J_z, J_x]_3 &=& -i\hbar^3 J_y \\
\vdots &=& \vdots
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-am39}
so that
$$
e^{-iJ_z\phi}J_xe^{iJ_z\phi} = J_x + \frac{i\phi}{\hbar}
(i\hbar J_y) + \left(\frac{i\phi}{\hbar}\right)^2(-i\hbar)^2(-J_x)
+ \left(\frac{i\phi}{\hbar}\right)^3(i\hbar)^3(-J_y) + \ldots.
$$
Getting together the real and the imaginary parts together, we get
$$
e^{iJ_z\phi/\hbar}J_xe^{-iJ_z\phi/\hbar} = J_x\left(1 - \frac{\phi^2}{2!}
+ \cdots\right) - J_y\left(\phi - \frac{\phi^3}{3!} + \cdots\right)
$$
or
$$
e^{iJ_z\phi/\hbar}J_xe^{-iJ_z\phi/\hbar} = J_x\cos\phi - J_y\sin\phi.
$$ {#eq-am40}
We can similarly show that
$$
\begin{eqnarray}
e^{iJ_z\phi/\hbar}J_ye^{-iJ_z\phi/\hbar} &=& J_x\sin\phi + J_y\cos\phi \\
e^{iJ_z\phi/\hbar}J_ze^{-iJ_z\phi/\hbar} &=& J_z 
\end{eqnarray}
$$ {#eq-am41}
Equations @eq-am40 and @eq-am41 are just the components of @eq-am36.

### Effect of rotation on spin - III
Consider an arbitrary state $\ket{\alpha}$ of a spin-$1/2$ system. We can
write it terms of the basis states $\{\ket{u}, \ket{d}\}$ as
$$
\ket{\alpha} = \braket{u|\alpha}\ket{u} + \braket{d|\alpha}\ket{d}
$$ {#eq-am42}
Let us rotate this state about the $z$-axis by an angle $\phi$. We can describe
the operation by applying the $D_z(\phi)$ operator on $\ket{\alpha}$. From
equation @eq-am17, we know that $D_z(\phi) = \exp(-iS_z\phi/\hbar)$ so that
$$
D_z(\phi)\ket{\alpha} = \braket{u|\alpha}e^{-iS_z\phi/\hbar}\ket{u} +
\braket{d|\alpha}e^{-iS_z\phi/\hbar}\ket{d}
$$ {#eq-am43}

Now,
$$
e^{-iS_z\phi/\hbar}\ket{u} = \sum_{k \ge 0}\left(\frac{-iS_z}{\hbar}\right)^k
\ket{u} = \sum_{k \ge 0}\left(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\right)^k
\left(\frac{\hbar}{2}\right)^k\ket{u} = e^{-i\phi/2}\ket{u},
$$ {#eq-am44}
where we used @eq-am24
Similarly,
$$
e^{-iS_z\phi/\hbar}\ket{d} = e^{i\phi/2}\ket{d}
$$ {#eq-am45}
so that @eq-am43 becomes
$$
D_z(\phi)\ket{\alpha} = \braket{u|\alpha}e^{-i\phi/2}\ket{u} + 
\braket{d|\alpha}e^{i\phi/2} \ket{d}.
$$ {#eq-am46}
In particular, $D_z(2\pi)\ket{\alpha} = -\ket{\alpha}$ and $D_z(4\pi)
\ket{\alpha} = \ket{\alpha}$. This, if we rotate a spin-$1/2$ system by $2\pi$,
we get its negative and that we have to rotate it twice over to get it back.
